proposals.name: Diagnoses specific mechanism behind prior failure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a precise technical/causal reason existing methods underperform in the target setting (a specific mismatch, invalid assumption, or missing signal) and ties the proposed fix directly to that diagnosis. Score 0 if it only asserts prior work 'has limitations,' 'lacks X,' or 'is insufficient' without explaining the underlying mechanism causing the shortfall.
proposals.rationale: R01 pinpoints a 'mismatch between refined Gaussian conditional and hyperprior distributions' causing rate-cost degradation, then proposes a regularizer targeting exactly that; R24 explains that pitch alone 'cannot fully represent the range of paralinguistic attributes,' motivating a learned alternative. Both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting dense rewards causal diagnosis that a term-matching scorecard conflates with generic 'gap' language (cf. R48's vaguer framing).

proposals.name: Unifies disparate tasks under one abstraction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reframes the problem so multiple previously-separate tasks or domains become instances of one underlying formalism, and shows this unification empirically or theoretically. Score 0 if it describes a method for one narrow task with no attempt to connect it to a broader class of problems.
proposals.rationale: R12's 'traveling observer' model treats arbitrary prediction tasks as measurements in a shared embedding space and shows it 'exploit[s] regularities across seemingly unrelated tasks'; R39 builds 'a unifying framework based on prover-verifier games' that 'generalises previously proposed interaction protocols.' Both dense_high_card_low, pointing to a synthesis quality a per-feature scorecard likely misses.

proposals.name: Reports a deliberately weaker baseline for honesty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract voluntarily reports how a simpler/naive competing approach performs (an ablation, random search, or an early/partial result) alongside the main method, even when it narrows the claimed advantage. Score 0 if it reports only comparisons against strong SOTA baselines with no acknowledgment of a simpler alternative.
proposals.rationale: R46 reports random search comes within '0.3% ... whilst reducing the search time from 36 hours down to 1 hour' of its evolutionary method; R56 candidly labels its results 'early training results.' Both dense_high_card_low; this self-undercutting honesty likely reads as credibility to a holistic dense judge but isn't captured by a scorecard rewarding stated superiority.

proposals.name: States formal guarantee integral to the claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract states a proof, bound, or certified guarantee (e.g., regret bound, convergence proof, certified robustness) that is load-bearing for the main contribution. Score 0 if no formal guarantee is mentioned, or 'theoretical' results are asserted without specifying what is proven.
proposals.rationale: R22 proves DOPL 'yields a sublinear regret' with an explicit rate, the 'first algorithm' to do so for its setting; R51 proves convergence 'to the global optimal value ... under mild conditions.' Both dense_high_card_low, versus e.g. R04's vaguer 'theoretically, we show that the performance ... depends on ...' which never states what is proven.

proposals.name: Translates outside-field grounding into mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract draws on a concrete finding or constraint from a non-ML field (biology, neuroscience, physics, developmental psychology) and shows precisely how it shapes a modeling choice. Score 0 if a real-world domain is mentioned only as an application label with no technical mechanism derived from it.
proposals.rationale: R35 imports the toy-duck/real-duck infant-learning distinction to motivate 'cluster-based metrics to quantify feature alignment'; R06 grounds CryoFM in structural-biology density-map statistics with flow matching fit to that data. Both dense_high_card_low; contrast R48, which invokes 'critical ecological challenges' as motivation without a technical mechanism tying ecology to environment design.

proposals.name: Quantitative claims are contextualized, not bare multipliers
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if every headline numeric claim states the comparison conditions (matched budget, same epsilon, named baseline, matched inputs) needed to interpret it. Score 0 if headline numbers are superlative (e.g., 'orders of magnitude,' extreme fps) with no stated comparison protocol or plausibility context.
proposals.rationale: R23 reports '1.24% RMSE ... 0.58% RMSE ... r = 0.94' against a precisely defined reconstruction target; R13 gives per-benchmark BLEU deltas 'over 2.6 BLEU improvement over the strong Transformer baseline.' Contrast R25's 'six orders of magnitude more accurate' and R17's '335.5 frames per second' (both dense_low_card_high), where claim scale is not anchored to a stated, checkable protocol.

proposals.name: Analyzes which component drives the improvement
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports an ablation, probing, or layer/component-wise analysis identifying which specific part of the system is responsible for the gain. Score 0 if only end-to-end aggregate numbers are reported with no attribution to a specific component.
proposals.rationale: R34 conducts 'an extensive investigation into the effectiveness of different vision encoders,' isolating that 'shallow layer features of CLIP' specifically help fine-grained tasks; R45 adds 'probing experiments' showing K-Adapter 'captures richer factual and commonsense knowledge.' Both dense_high_card_low, suggesting dense rewards demonstrated understanding of internals over an unexplained aggregate win.

proposals.name: Poses a sharp, falsifiable research question
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract states an explicit, answerable question or hypothesis that structures the investigation, and the rest of the abstract addresses it. Score 0 if it states only a general goal or capability ('we improve X') with no explicit question being tested.
proposals.rationale: R15 explicitly asks 'would it be more effective to separate highly conflicting objectives into different optimization levels or keep them in one level?' and structures a three-framework comparison around answering it; R05 states 'can these existing research efforts actually effectively achieve the desired system-level attack effects ...?' as its driving question. R15 is dense_high_card_low and R05 is dense_low_card_high, so this signal cuts across the disagreement direction -- evidence it is a real quality marker the scorecard bank may underweight broadly.

proposals.name: Benchmark validity grounded in a statistical model
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if, for a dataset/benchmark contribution, the abstract grounds its validity claim in an explicit statistical or measurement-theoretic model (e.g., a latent-ability estimator, correlation with a known criterion, reconstruction error against the full instrument). Score 0 if the benchmark contribution is justified only by pipeline/engineering claims (e.g., '% samples removed,' '% time saved') with no validity model.
proposals.rationale: R23's metabench derives 'estimators of the underlying benchmark-specific abilities' and reports reconstruction RMSE plus a correlation of r=.94 with the full-benchmark score; contrast R59's LIME, justified via 'reduces the number of samples by 76% and evaluation time by 77%' from a 'semi-automated pipeline' with no comparable validity argument. R23 is dense_high_card_low while R59 is strongly dense_low_card_high -- a sharp within-task contrast (both are benchmark-compression papers) a term-based scorecard likely can't distinguish.

proposals.name: Motivating gap is technically specific, not templated
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract's opening problem statement names a precise technical shortcoming (a specific failure mode, quantity, or unhandled case). Score 0 if the opening uses generic template language ('however, X remains underexplored/overlooked/challenging') without specifying what technically breaks.
proposals.rationale: R01 opens by specifying that 'latent refinement ... is barely tailored to cross-domain scenarios' and later names the exact distributional mismatch; R06 specifies processing 'has yet to fully benefit from our knowledge of biomolecular density maps.' Contrast R14's 'it remains nontrivial to evaluate ... for reasons including (1)...(2)...(3)' and R48's 'it is unclear if the findings equip for real-world problems' (both dense_low_card_high), which gesture at a gap without technical specificity.

proposals.name: Restrained vs stakes-inflating language about importance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract conveys the work's importance entirely through precise technical description, with no appeals to broad urgency, moral stakes, or rhetorical framing. Score 0 if it uses charged/rhetorical language about risk, urgency, or moral importance ('whistleblower,' 'advocates,' 'critical,' 'pressure grows') in place of, or alongside, technical specificity.
proposals.rationale: R21 frames its contribution as acting 'as a whistleblower for the community' and 'advocates for the adoption of more advanced techniques'; R48 (HIVEX) opens with 'critical ecological challenges' and 'pressure grows' before describing a fairly standard multi-agent RL environment suite. Both are dense_low_card_high rows, suggesting a scorecard may over-credit urgency framing that a holistic dense reader discounts relative to technical content.

proposals.name: Explicit trade-off framing with quantified position
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific two-sided trade-off central to the problem and states, with a number, where the proposed method lands on that trade-off relative to an alternative. Score 0 if no trade-off is named, or a trade-off is claimed 'solved' with no quantified position on it.
proposals.rationale: R11 explicitly frames the 'privacy and utility' trade-off and quantifies its position ('75% accuracy on CIFAR10 when using only 2,000 public images' at a stated privacy budget); R38 frames a memory-vs-compute trade-off and quantifies both sides ('3x' memory reduction 'with a 9-16% overhead'). Both dense_low_card_high, indicating the scorecard may reward explicit trade-off quantification that dense's holistic read weighs less heavily.

proposals.name: Qualifies or revisits a prior claim with evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly states that it contradicts, revises, or adds a boundary condition to a specific prior finding or common assumption, supported by a stated result. Score 0 if it makes no reference to any specific prior claim being revised and only claims improvement over baselines.
proposals.rationale: R36 states that sampling above the standard bootstrap rate 'has generally proven ineffective' in prior literature but here yields improvements 'contrary to previous findings'; R05 shows prior physical adversarial attacks 'cannot achieve any system-level effect' despite being assumed effective at the component level. Both dense_low_card_high, indicating the scorecard rewards assumption-revision that dense may be under-weighting relative to raw novelty.

proposals.name: Reports generalization across heterogeneous conditions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports results broken out across multiple qualitatively different conditions (languages, sensor configurations, domains, architectures) with per-condition findings, not just an aggregate. Score 0 if it reports a single aggregate result on one setting/dataset.
proposals.rationale: R19 evaluates across 'three key dimensions' and 'four different input languages,' reporting differentiated findings by prompt complexity; R09 shows versatility 'by estimating movement dynamics for a variety of sparse sensor configurations.' R19 is dense_high_card_low while R09 is dense_low_card_high, showing this signal appears on both sides -- a scorecard likely catches real per-axis generalization evidence that dense's holistic read treats inconsistently.

proposals.name: Experimental setup is specific enough to verify
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names concrete, checkable specifics of the experimental setup (exact dataset names, sample sizes, number of items/models evaluated, released artifacts). Score 0 if experiments are referred to only in generic terms ('extensive experiments,' 'various datasets,' 'experiments show') without naming what was actually run.
proposals.rationale: R23 specifies 'data from n > 5000 LLMs,' six named benchmarks, and 'd = 28,632 items in total'; R44 names the exact dataset (CerebroVoice), languages, and release venues ('publicly available on Zenodo and GitHub'). Contrast R30's 'The experiments show that the proposed method converges faster ... while requiring half the parameters' with no dataset named at all -- R30 is dense_low_card_high despite an unverifiable setup, a distinction dense apparently tracks more reliably than the scorecard.

proposals.name: Mechanism-level account of why the method works
proposals.instruction: Score how far the abstract explains the causal reason its method works, not merely what the method is. 10: a specific failure mode or structural property is named and a specific design choice is shown to act on exactly that property, such that a reader could predict when the method would stop working (e.g. a mismatch between a refined conditional and a hyperprior is identified and the added regularizer targets precisely that mismatch; certain sub-paths are argued not to change the semantic level of features and are therefore shown to be skippable; demo clustering is motivated by a stated connection between in-context learning and kernel regression). 5: a plausible intuition is offered, but the link from design to effect is asserted rather than argued. 0: the method is presented only as a sequence of named stages or modules, with effectiveness attributed to the modules simply existing.
proposals.rationale: This is the sharpest axis separating the two halves. R43 and R44 sit at dense_pct 0.68/0.75 with card_pct 0.19/0.28, and both spend their central sentences deriving a mechanism (marginalization mismatch; sub-paths that refine but do not shift semantic level). R09 and R07 do the same (residual/layer-norm stability; kernel-regression grounding for demo assignment). By contrast R16 (card 0.699, dense 0.156) and R33 (card 0.621, dense 0.058) enumerate branded components (IUR/ICL; semantic tokens, single-quantizer codec, hierarchical modeling, token chain prompting) without saying why any of them should help. A scorecard built from presence-of-method-description credits R16 and R33 fully and cannot see what R43 and R44 are doing.

proposals.name: Specific, checkable diagnosis of prior work's failure
proposals.instruction: Score how precisely the abstract locates where and why existing approaches break, in terms a reader could go and check. 10: the deficiency is stated as a concrete property of prior systems (they treat observed and target points separately; stagewise training cannot evaluate full-model performance in early stages; existing pipelines extract features only from deep CLIP layers; prior evaluations occur at the component level and never at the system level). 0: prior work is dismissed with generic deficits — lacks interpretability, lacks robustness, limited performance, remains challenging, remains underexplored — with no identified cause and nothing a reader could falsify.
proposals.rationale: R09 (dense 0.849 / card 0.347) and R55 (dense 0.732 / card 0.158) each open by naming an exact, checkable defect in the incumbent method, and their proposed fix is legible as the complement of that defect. R43 (dense 0.683 / card 0.193) goes further and proves the defect. Against this, R18 (dense 0.038 / card 0.871) motivates with 'they lack interpretability and robustness' and R16 (dense 0.156 / card 0.699) with generic uncertainty and bias language; both are well-formed abstracts that a checklist scores highly, but the diagnosis is unfalsifiable from the text.

proposals.name: Reframes the problem versus increments an existing pipeline
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work changes what question the field asks or adds a delta to a named existing system. 10: the abstract introduces a new object of study, formulation, or evaluation regime — prediction recast as an observer measuring a shared space; evaluation shifted from deterministic point estimates to guarantees over the output distribution; a bandit model where only pairwise preference, not scalar reward, is observed; a unifying framework that generalises previously proposed interaction protocols. 0: an extra module, extra iteration, extra loss, or extra stage is bolted onto a specifically named prior system and the resulting delta is reported.
proposals.rationale: R08 (dense 0.704 / card 0.202), R52 (dense 0.704 / card 0.201), R59 (dense 0.771 / card 0.270) and R27 (dense 0.794 / card 0.297) all reformulate rather than increment, and all four are penalised by the scorecard. R11 (dense 0.010 / card 0.912) is the clean opposite: auto-regressive iteration added to AdvGAN, scored near the top of the card. R53 (dense 0.088 / card 0.728) bolts a diffusion model onto demonstration ordering. Reformulation is invisible to a bank of per-property questions because each individual property of R11 is satisfied.

proposals.name: Reports a counterintuitive finding, not only a win
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract reports a result that contradicts a standard assumption, stated as a finding in its own right. 10: a prior belief is overturned and the overturning is the headline — shallow layers outperform deep ones for fine-grained tasks and a text-free vision model beats the image-text-aligned one; six large benchmarks compress to under 3% of their size with a single common factor; deterministic evaluation falsely certifies successful unlearning and alignment; a widely reported per-dimension metric turns out to be inadequate and is better excluded. 0: every result reported is that the authors' own system scored higher than the alternatives.
proposals.rationale: R55 (dense 0.732 / card 0.158) and R23 (dense 0.787 / card 0.296) and R52 (dense 0.704 / card 0.201) each carry a finding that would change a reader's behaviour even if the reader never uses the proposed artifact; all three are card-suppressed. R39 (dense 0.031 / card 0.880) and R33 (dense 0.058 / card 0.621) report only that their method wins, across many datasets, and score at the top of the card. A criterion bank keyed to 'are results reported' cannot distinguish a result from a scoreboard entry.

proposals.name: Claim calibration: stated scope limits and self-deflating evidence
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract voluntarily bounds its own claims or reports evidence that weakens its own pitch. 10: the authors mark the limits themselves — early training results, preliminary computational experiments, a semi-realistic network of 95k parameters, competitive rather than superior, or a reported control that nearly matches the proposed method. 0: unqualified superlatives throughout, with consistently / significantly / state-of-the-art / substantially attached to every result and no stated boundary anywhere.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense 0.635 / card 0.050), R56 (dense 0.683 / card 0.180), R24 (dense 0.764 / card 0.258) and R51 (dense 0.615 / card 0.040) all discount themselves in the abstract; R51 even reports that random search comes within 0.3% top-1 at a 36x lower search cost. These are the four lowest card scores in the dense_high half, so the scorecard is almost certainly reading hedges as missing strength. R39 (card 0.880) and R10 (card 0.613) and R33 (card 0.621) hedge nothing and are rewarded. A careful reviewer reads voluntary discounting as a signal the authors know their own evidence.

proposals.name: Theory is load-bearing rather than decorative
proposals.instruction: Score whether stated theory has content and does work in the argument. 10: the theoretical result is stated with its substance and something depends on it — a named regret rate that is itself the contribution, a convergence-to-global-optimum guarantee under stated conditions, a stability characterization that explains why the proposed training schedule is safe, a formal comparison of competing protocols. 0: theory is invoked without content — a provable strategy, an analysis extending previous findings to a larger space, an NP-hardness remark — and no claim in the abstract would change if the theory were removed.
proposals.rationale: R59 (dense 0.771 / card 0.270) and R24 (dense 0.764 / card 0.258) state theory whose removal would gut the paper. R10 (dense 0.073 / card 0.613) says 'provable pessimism-based strategy' and then offers only that performance depends on LLM quality and distribution matching; R39 (dense 0.031 / card 0.880) says a theoretical analysis extends prior generalization findings to infinite dimensions without saying what it concludes; R25 (dense 0.116 / card 0.669) invokes NP-hardness decoratively. A bank item asking 'is there theoretical analysis?' scores R10 and R39 identically to R59 and R24.

proposals.name: Comparison holds a resource or budget constant
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract states what was equalized in its comparisons. 10: the controlled quantity is explicit — competitive at similar FLOPs, or 20-33% fewer FLOPs at better loss; the same privacy budget and the same number of public data points; a stated 2x reduction in learnable parameters against the incumbent fine-tuning method; the same search budget or an explicit search-time reduction. 0: outperformance is claimed with nothing stated as held fixed, so a reader cannot tell whether the gain came from the idea or from additional compute, data, parameters, or training signal.
proposals.rationale: R09 (dense 0.849 / card 0.347), R40 (dense 0.249 / card 0.768 — the exception that shows the axis is not simply a proxy for the split), R37 (dense 0.700 / card 0.134) and R51 (dense 0.615 / card 0.040) all name the invariant. R33 (card 0.621), R16 (card 0.699) and R11 (card 0.912) claim state-of-the-art with no invariant stated at all and are among the highest card scores in the slice. Cost-matching is the difference between a claim and a scoreboard, and a checklist that asks only 'are baselines compared?' cannot see it.

proposals.name: Extraordinary headline numbers accounted for
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score the joint condition: the size of the reported gain TOGETHER WITH whether the abstract accounts for that size. 10: either the gains are modest and precisely scoped, or an unusually large gain is paired with a structural reason it is that large — what the baseline could not represent, what changed in the problem setup. 0: an order-of-magnitude or otherwise extraordinary claim is asserted with no account of where the margin comes from (an MAE roughly 14x smaller than the state of the art; six orders of magnitude more accurate in tail energy; hundreds of frames per second against gradient-based attacks), leaving the comparison unauditable from the abstract alone.
proposals.rationale: R01 (dense 0.035 / card 0.835) and R45 (dense 0.200 / card 0.787) and R11 (dense 0.019 / card 0.912) are the three most numerically spectacular abstracts in the slice and three of the lowest dense percentiles in it. Each supplies a jaw-dropping ratio with no mechanism for its magnitude. Compare R09 and R37, where the numbers are smaller and every one is tied to a held-constant quantity. A criterion bank that rewards 'quantitative results are reported' will reward exactly the unauditable magnitudes hardest.

proposals.name: Central idea legible in one sentence
proposals.instruction: Score whether a reader can restate the core lever in one sentence after one reading, and whether that lever is a single coherent change. 10: the contribution reduces cleanly — mask randomly chosen past tokens during next-token prediction; use one pointer head for localization and one for repair and train them jointly; run multiple primal and dual models instead of one pair; three stated simple ideas whose combination is the algorithm. 0: the method is a stack of separately branded sub-components whose relationship to one another is never stated, so the contribution cannot be summarized without reciting acronyms.
proposals.rationale: R50 (dense 0.753 / card 0.059), R49 (dense 0.808 / card 0.235), R04 (dense 0.791 / card 0.113) and R28 (dense 0.744 / card 0.273) are all compressible to one clause, and all four are card-suppressed — plausibly because a short, single-lever abstract fails per-property completeness questions. R16 (IUR + ICL), R33 (four named stages) and R48 (dataset + two benchmarks + MoBSE + a VAD finding) accumulate components and score 0.699/0.621/0.917 on the card. Component count is easy to score; conceptual compression is not.

proposals.name: Evidence-carrying language rather than self-promotion
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of stated results to asserted importance. 10: claims are flat and every adjective does work; the reader is told what happened and is left to judge significance. 0: the abstract asserts its own novelty and impact in place of reporting — innovative, novel repeated across sentences, the first of its kind, empowering researchers and practitioners, paving the way for future advancements, shedding light on the potential, acting as a whistleblower for the community — with the promotional sentences occupying space that no result occupies.
proposals.rationale: R14 (dense 0.096 / card 0.631) closes on 'empower researchers... paving the way'; R10 (dense 0.073 / card 0.613) closes on 'shedding light on the potential'; R06 (dense 0.090 / card 0.863) casts itself as a whistleblower; R02 (dense 0.194 / card 0.949, the highest card score in the slice) uses novel twice in two sentences. All four are bottom-quintile on dense. R49, R51 and R28 state results and stop. Promotional prose reads to a checklist as a stated contribution and to a careful reader as a substitute for one.

proposals.name: Evaluation breadth together with a mechanism-isolating experiment
proposals.instruction: Composite. Score breadth of evaluation TOGETHER WITH the presence of at least one experiment that isolates the proposed mechanism. 10: alongside whatever datasets and baselines are used, the abstract describes a probe, ablation, control, or trivial-alternative comparison that could locate the source of the gain — probing that the injected adapters carry more factual and commonsense knowledge than the base model; showing that simpler representations of the inverse Hessian degrade performance; reporting what random search achieves; systematically varying the two candidate signals to see which drives the effect. 0: the evaluation is characterized only as extensive or comprehensive across N datasets and M baselines, with no experiment that could distinguish the proposed mechanism from any other source of improvement.
proposals.rationale: R32 (dense 0.864 / card 0.225), R56 (dense 0.683 / card 0.180), R51 (dense 0.615 / card 0.040) and R47 (dense 0.581 / card 0.065) each describe an experiment aimed at the mechanism rather than the leaderboard, and all four are heavily card-suppressed. R39 (seven baselines, 19 datasets, card 0.880), R02 (five real-world datasets, card 0.949) and R54 (25 MLLMs, card 0.720) offer breadth with no isolating experiment and score at the very top. Dataset and baseline counts are trivially scorable; diagnostic intent is not.

proposals.name: Question posed could have come out the other way
proposals.instruction: Score whether the study as described had a possible outcome other than 'our method wins'. 10: a genuine open question is posed and the answer reported, including when the answer is unflattering — is it better to separate highly conflicting objectives into different optimization levels or keep them in one; how do two candidate learning signals interact to affect cross-domain alignment; do the leading models actually succeed at this generation task (answer: all of them struggle, and the evaluation is run by domain experts). 0: the described design admits exactly one outcome, because the only quantity reported is whether the authors' system beat the alternatives.
proposals.rationale: R46 (dense 0.573 / card 0.065) and R47 (dense 0.581 / card 0.065) are the two lowest card scores among the dense_high half, and both are framed as investigations with no guaranteed winner and no SOTA claim — precisely the shape a scorecard reads as 'no demonstrated improvement'. R36 (dense 0.864 / card 0.363) reports that every evaluated model, including its own strongest, fails on the harder prompts. R16, R39 and R60 admit only one outcome and score 0.699/0.880/0.793. Falsifiable framing is a quality signal that a win-oriented bank inverts.

proposals.name: Engages the target domain's real constraints
proposals.instruction: Score whether domain importance is demonstrated through specifics or merely asserted. 10: the domain's actual constraints visibly shape the work — data gathered by an instrument currently operating on Mars; roughly 40k existing density maps that current processing algorithms fail to exploit and a model built to exploit exactly that prior; an evaluation carried out by eleven domain scientists across stated criteria; an expensive black-box objective with cheaper approximations of differing fidelity. 0: real-world stakes are asserted in the framing (critical ecological challenges, clinical applications, real-world problems) but no domain-specific constraint, quantity, instrument, or expert judgement appears anywhere in the abstract.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense 0.635 / card 0.050), R41 (dense 0.818 / card 0.259), R36 (dense 0.864 / card 0.363) and R20 (dense 0.871 / card 0.398) each let the domain constrain the design and are all card-suppressed. R19 (dense 0.038 / card 0.654) and R14 (dense 0.096 / card 0.631) assert real-world urgency at length — ecological challenges, mobile network management — while remaining entirely generic about the constraints, and the card credits the assertion. This axis matters because 'is the problem well motivated?' is easy to satisfy rhetorically and hard to satisfy substantively.

proposals.name: Technical prose precision and naming discipline
proposals.instruction: Score the exactness of the writing itself. 10: sentences are grammatical, terms are defined before use, quantities carry units or referents, and the method's name is a plain label. 0: the core claim contains grammatical breakage (a method described as 'incorporating maximize Q-function'), undefined jargon is stacked into unparseable noun phrases, or the system name is a forced backronym with letters typographically extracted out of a phrase mid-sentence.
proposals.rationale: R34 (dense 0.123 / card 0.767) and R02 (dense 0.194 / card 0.949) are the two most typographically and grammatically damaged abstracts in the slice and score 0.77 and 0.95 on the card — a judge answering per-property questions reads past the prose. R23 (dense 0.787), R27 (dense 0.794) and R08 (dense 0.704) are exact throughout and card-suppressed. Prose precision is one of the strongest cheap correlates of care taken with everything else, and it is exactly the kind of gestalt property an itemized bank decomposes away.

proposals.name: Ambition of the research bet
proposals.instruction: Score how much was risked. 10: the paper commits to a hard target where failure was a live possibility — globally solving a class of mixed-integer nonlinear programs that existing solvers cannot even model, a protocol for a bounded verifier to learn from untrusted powerful provers, a first foundation model for a scientific modality that has none, autonomous navigation learned from data returned by a rover on another planet. 5: a substantive but well-trodden target. 0: a safe increment inside a saturated setting where a small positive delta was close to assured before the work began.
proposals.rationale: R24 (dense 0.764 / card 0.258), R27 (dense 0.794 / card 0.297), R41 (dense 0.818 / card 0.259) and R03 (dense 0.635 / card 0.050) all take bets that could plainly have failed, and all four are card-suppressed. R11 (dense 0.019 / card 0.912), R16 (dense 0.156 / card 0.699) and R60 (dense 0.159 / card 0.793) are low-risk increments on established recipes and sit at the top of the card. Risk taken is not a property of any single sentence, so a per-property bank cannot assemble it; a reader perceives it immediately.

proposals.name: Algorithmic Novelty vs. Data Provision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract introduces a fundamentally new algorithm, mathematical formulation, or model architecture as its primary contribution. Score 0 if it only provides a new dataset, benchmark, or empirical study without any algorithmic innovation.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards algorithmic breakthroughs (R01, R40) but penalizes pure dataset or benchmark creation (R02, R12) which the scorecard seems to over-credit.

proposals.name: Explicit Theoretical Guarantees
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper explicitly states formal mathematical proofs, regret bounds, or rigorous theoretical guarantees. Score 0 if it is entirely empirical or heuristic with no mention of theoretical properties.
proposals.rationale: Dense heavily favors theory-backed methods (R09, R39), while the scorecard gives high scores to purely heuristic or empirical tweaks (R47, R56) that lack such guarantees.

proposals.name: Conceptual Framework Unification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the work unifies previously disjoint tasks or methodologies into a single, elegant conceptual framework. Score 0 if it addresses a hyper-specific problem with a bespoke, non-generalizable solution.
proposals.rationale: Abstracts that introduce unifying perspectives score highly under the dense model (R01, R50), whereas the scorecard misses this and seems to reward narrow, bespoke solutions (R10, R38).

proposals.name: Paradigm-Limitation Identification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract identifies a fundamental flaw in standard evaluation, training, or methodology and proposes a principled fix. Score 0 if it applies standard paradigms without any meta-level critique.
proposals.rationale: Dense highly values papers that rethink how we evaluate or understand models (R35, R60), a property the scorecard completely misses.

proposals.name: Domain-Integrated Methodological Innovation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a novel ML algorithm is explicitly designed to solve a high-impact scientific problem where standard ML fails. Score 0 if existing standard ML architectures are simply applied to a new domain dataset.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards methodological innovations tailored to scientific domains (R42, R44) but penalizes papers that just apply standard nets to new data (R36, R59); the scorecard over-credits the domain itself.

proposals.name: Parsimonious Methodological Elegance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a complex problem is solved with a surprisingly simple, lightweight modification yielding strong results. Score 0 if results rely heavily on overly complex, multi-stage architectures or brute-force tuning.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values elegant solutions (R15, R49), while the scorecard over-credits unnecessary complexity and jargon-heavy multi-model stacking (R57, R58).

proposals.name: Reliance on Pre-existing Closed Models
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper develops and trains new models from scratch or via fundamental architectural changes. Score 0 if it relies entirely on prompting or wrapping pre-existing closed-source models.
proposals.rationale: Dense penalizes abstracts that primarily act as wrappers around existing LLMs (R25, R55), whereas the scorecard may over-credit the downstream task performance.

proposals.name: Definitive Quantitative Superiority
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports definitive, large-margin improvements or sets new state-of-the-art records. Score 0 if it shows only marginal, within-margin improvements or lacks proper baselines.
proposals.rationale: Dense favors unambiguous quantitative superiority (R48, R21), while the scorecard gives high scores to abstracts lacking strong baselines or clear improvements (R52, R12).

proposals.name: Lexical Obfuscation vs. Clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if standard terminology is used and novel concepts are explained intuitively. Score 0 if the text relies on excessive proprietary jargon or convoluted phrasing that obscures the mechanism.
proposals.rationale: Dense rewards clarity (R15, R49), whereas abstracts stacking buzzwords (e.g., 'Semantic Field Subspace' R57, 'pessimism-based strategy' R56) trick the scorecard into assigning high scores.

proposals.name: Cognitive/Scientific Principle Extraction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a general ML principle is rigorously extracted from a deep interdisciplinary analogy (e.g., cognitive science). Score 0 if biological or physical inspiration is used merely as a superficial buzzword.
proposals.rationale: Dense values deep interdisciplinary transfer, such as taking inspiration from infant learning to propose new metrics (R18), but penalizes biological analogies that fail to yield practical ML advances (R19).

proposals.name: Framework vs. Systems Engineering
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution is a new learning algorithm, theoretical framework, or mathematical model. Score 0 if the focus is primarily on systems engineering, software libraries, or simulation environments.
proposals.rationale: Dense heavily penalizes pure systems engineering or environment creation (R33, R52), which the scorecard rates highly due to surface-level thoroughness.

proposals.name: Cross-Domain Generalizability of Method
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed method is explicitly shown to generalize across fundamentally different domains, architectures, or datasets. Score 0 if the method is hyper-specific to a single narrow task.
proposals.rationale: Dense favors methods proving utility across multiple distinct domains (R03, R05), while the scorecard misses this value, rewarding narrow setups (R47, R59).

proposals.name: Fundamental Representation Learning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method improves the core underlying representation learning mechanism (e.g., latent space structuring). Score 0 if it relies on task-specific architectural hacks or post-processing.
proposals.rationale: Dense rates abstracts that fundamentally improve data representation highly (R54, R45), while dense_low_card_high papers rely on task-specific engineering (R46, R53) that the scorecard over-credits.

proposals.name: Algorithmic Step-Change vs. Incremental Tuning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the contribution represents a significant step-change in methodology. Score 0 if it represents incremental hyperparameter tuning or minor modifications to existing algorithms.
proposals.rationale: Dense penalizes papers making very narrow empirical adjustments (R47, R38), whereas the scorecard seems to over-credit them as valid contributions.

proposals.name: Novel Formal Problem Formulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper mathematically formulates a completely new problem or reformulates an existing problem in a transformative way. Score 0 if it addresses a heavily studied, standard problem.
proposals.rationale: Dense places high value on the formal introduction of new problems (R09, R50), a property the scorecard misses, favoring instead papers that apply standard formulations to new data (R02, R13).

proposals.name: Mechanistic Transparency of Proposed Method
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly details the mathematical, architectural, or algorithmic mechanism of the proposed method (e.g., explains exactly *how* a loss function or architectural change works). Score 0 if the abstract relies entirely on vague high-level descriptors (e.g., 'novel mapping', 'innovative framework') without explaining the underlying mechanism.
proposals.rationale: The dense model may highly value clear technical mechanistic descriptions over generic claims. R03 and R14 explicitly explain their mechanisms (training subnetworks, masking past tokens), whereas R20 and R24 use vague buzzwords ('Semantic Field Subspace', 'novel type of generative model') that the scorecard might mistakenly reward.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Precision of Prior Flaws
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract pinpoints the exact technical or theoretical failure mode in prior work that the paper addresses. Score 0 if the abstract only uses generic boilerplate to dismiss prior work (e.g., 'existing methods are inefficient' or 'face challenges').
proposals.rationale: The dense model likely perceives quality through deep problem diagnosis. R15 and R48 specifically diagnose flaws in enumerative repairs and RL stitching, while R16 and R26 rely on broad statements about prior methods being 'data inefficient' or lacking semantic analysis.

proposals.name: Conceptual Problem Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper fundamentally reframes the problem domain or introduces a new conceptual paradigm (e.g., shifting from point estimates to probabilistic evaluations). Score 0 if the paper treats an existing, well-known framework as given and merely proposes a minor tweak to it.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values paradigm shifts. R04 and R42 reframe evaluation and general prediction systems entirely, explaining their high dense scores, whereas R02 and R23 operate entirely within standard established frameworks (Random Forests, long-tailed recognition) yet achieve high scorecard scores.

proposals.name: Quantitative Specificity of Empirical Gains
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract provides exact numerical improvements, resource trade-offs, or specific deltas (e.g., 'improves by 5.7% accuracy', 'reduces FLOPs by 20-33%'). Score 0 if empirical results are described solely through subjective qualifiers like 'significant improvements', 'superior performance', or 'state-of-the-art results'.
proposals.rationale: Scorecards may over-credit the mere presence of buzzwords like 'state-of-the-art'. The dense model seems to prefer quantifiable evidence, as seen in R14 and R60, while penalizing vague claims of superiority found in R23 and R27.

proposals.name: Methodological vs. Domain Novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core contribution is a fundamental machine learning algorithm, architecture, or mathematical framework. Score 0 if the primary contribution is merely applying existing ML techniques to a new application domain or curating a new dataset for it.
proposals.rationale: The dense model prioritizes core ML advancements over domain application papers. R10 and R21 introduce fundamental ML architectural changes, while R25 and R54 (dense low, card high) primarily contribute new datasets or apply existing methods to new fields (medical imaging, mobile networks).

proposals.name: Algorithmic Parsimony and Elegance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed solution is described as simple, minimal, or avoiding complex pipelines while solving a hard problem. Score 0 if the method requires stitching together multiple disjoint heavy modules, convoluted multi-stage pipelines, or esoteric heuristics.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors elegant, unifying solutions over engineered complexity. R47 and R56 emphasize simple, minimal changes for high impact, whereas R44 and R58 describe highly convoluted, multi-stage frameworks that the scorecard might over-credit.

proposals.name: Objective Tone and Absence of Hype
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract maintains a strictly objective, measured scientific tone. Score 0 if the abstract overuses dramatic adjectives (e.g., 'immense', 'remarkable', 'critical', 'whistleblower') or uses grandiose framing for routine contributions.
proposals.rationale: Overhyping is a negative quality signal that a dense end-to-end model might catch, but a checklist scorecard might miss. R01 and R55 use heavy dramatic framing and hype, while high-dense abstracts like R28 and R32 remain highly technical and objective.

proposals.name: Explicit Cost-Benefit Trade-off Articulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract clearly articulates a trade-off (e.g., 'reduces memory by 3x at the cost of 15% computation', or 'better alignment with 2x fewer parameters'). Score 0 if the abstract claims absolute improvements (e.g., 'faster and more accurate') without acknowledging or quantifying any associated costs or trade-offs.
proposals.rationale: Explicitly quantified trade-offs indicate rigorous empirical evaluation. R03 and R22 clearly define their cost-benefit ratios, whereas R06 and R46 make strong claims about memory/accuracy gains but frame them less rigorously.

proposals.name: Theory-Driven Algorithmic Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract shows that a formal mathematical theorem, theoretical bound, or proof directly motivated and shaped the proposed algorithm. Score 0 if theory is mentioned as a disconnected afterthought, or if the method is entirely heuristic without theoretical backing.
proposals.rationale: The dense model may detect when theory is integral versus superficial. In R05 and R31, theory directly informs the algorithmic design, whereas in R36 and R46, theory is mentioned as a general add-on to support an empirical heuristic.

proposals.name: Generality of the Proposed Principle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the core insight or proposed method is applicable across a wide array of tasks, domains, or architectures. Score 0 if the method is severely overfit to a hyper-specific sub-problem or a single niche configuration.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values broad impact. R04 and R29 provide frameworks that generalize across ML, while R02 and R17 focus on extremely narrow configurations (bootstrap rates in Random Forests, stitching in offline RL).

proposals.name: Specificity of Baseline Comparisons
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly names the specific baseline models or prior state-of-the-art techniques it compares against. Score 0 if the abstract only uses generic phrases like 'compared to previous methods' or 'outperforms state-of-the-art baselines'.
proposals.rationale: Naming baselines grounds the work in the existing literature. R08 and R19 explicitly list the models (GPT-4o, RoBERTa) they evaluate against, while R23 and R45 vaguely reference 'state-of-the-art' or 'previous methods'.

proposals.name: Depth of Scientific Domain Integration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract deeply integrates domain-specific scientific knowledge (e.g., physical laws, biological priors) into the ML objective, rather than just using the domain as a data source. Score 0 if the domain is treated superficially merely as a new dataset for a generic ML pipeline.
proposals.rationale: When domain papers are deemed high quality by the dense model, they respect the underlying science. R34 and R39 deeply embed cryo-EM and molecular constraints into their models, whereas R12 and R41 treat ecology or brain signals mostly as generic data sources.

proposals.name: Optimization Objective Formulation Clarity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract clearly specifies the mathematical or conceptual optimization objective, loss function, or reward signal being optimized. Score 0 if the abstract focuses entirely on architecture or data pipelines and completely omits the training objective.
proposals.rationale: Clearly stating what is being optimized is a hallmark of rigorous ML. R04 and R40 explicitly discuss their novel loss functions and objectives, while R20 and R57 talk extensively about embeddings and attacks but leave the optimization objective opaque.

proposals.name: Principled vs. Opportunistic Technique Combination
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract combines disparate techniques (e.g., two different ML paradigms) based on a deeply argued theoretical or conceptual motivation. Score 0 if it awkwardly stitches together trendy buzzwords (e.g., combining 'Diffusion Models' with 'LLMs') without a principled justification.
proposals.rationale: The dense model penalizes trendy mashups lacking solid grounding. R11 and R31 combine components based on rigorous mathematical mappings, while R35 and R37 stitch together concepts like diffusion models with theorem proving in a less principled manner.

proposals.name: Verifiability of Empirical Claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the claims made in the abstract are strictly measurable using standard, well-defined metrics (e.g., BLEU, Accuracy, RMSE). Score 0 if the primary claims rely on highly subjective metrics (e.g., 'more natural', 'better human alignment') without clear metric definitions.
proposals.rationale: Papers that rely on vague, subjective claims often lack rigor. R15 and R28 use strict verifiable metrics, whereas R41 and R52 rely heavily on qualitative or subjective claims like 'more natural and intelligible reconstructed speech'.

proposals.name: Mechanism-targeted problem solving
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a precise failure mode and each major design choice directly addresses it; score 0 when the motivation is generic and the method-to-problem connection is unexplained.
proposals.rationale: This pattern is prominent in R10, where joint localization and repair address enumeration, and R17, where learned paralinguistic codes address hand-engineered features.

proposals.name: Nontrivial component synergy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when multiple components have complementary roles whose interaction is essential to the claimed improvement; score 0 when components are merely listed or independently appended.
proposals.rationale: R05 describes adapters whose separation and combination support continual multi-knowledge infusion, while R21 explicitly constructs synergistic instruction-and-demonstration experts.

proposals.name: Theory-to-method guarantee alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a formal result directly explains or guarantees the central algorithmic behavior or claim; score 0 when theory is absent, generic, or disconnected from the method.
proposals.rationale: R02 ties theoretical guarantees to a nonstationary influence kernel, and R18 connects sublinear regret directly to preference-based decision making.

proposals.name: Structural transfer beyond training distribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method encodes a principled mechanism for handling unseen tasks, domains, objects, or inputs and demonstrates that transfer; score 0 when evaluation remains within the original setting.
proposals.rationale: R24 separates object-specific from object-agnostic structure for unseen shape completion, and R52 uses a shared representation to transfer across disjoint tasks.

proposals.name: Matched Pareto efficiency evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when quality improvements are compared under matched resource conditions and multiple relevant cost-quality axes are reported; score 0 when only an isolated performance number or vague efficiency claim is given.
proposals.rationale: R23 reports downstream gains alongside FLOP savings, R27 compares parameter efficiency with target alignment, and R43 measures accuracy against search time.

proposals.name: Assumption-challenging empirical discovery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states a surprising result that challenges a prevailing assumption and tests when or why it occurs; score 0 when novelty is only a contrarian headline without controlled evidence.
proposals.rationale: R22 finds DINO outperforming CLIP in fine-grained multimodal perception, while R28 shows randomly masking past tokens improves long-context representations.

proposals.name: End-to-end task validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation measures the complete downstream behavior relevant to the stated application, including interactions among system components; score 0 when only an intermediate proxy or isolated module metric is evaluated.
proposals.rationale: R07 validates planning with rover data, and R14 evaluates probabilistic behavior relevant to real unlearning and alignment rather than relying on point estimates.

proposals.name: Robustness across realistic variation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when results are consistent across meaningful domains, conditions, modalities, or deployment variations that test the method's intended scope; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrow standard setting.
proposals.rationale: R24 evaluates multiple shape domains, R41 covers both in-domain and cross-domain compression, and R60 studies several languages, tasks, and datasets.

proposals.name: Causal diagnostic evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when ablations, controlled comparisons, or systematic factor variations isolate which mechanism causes the result; score 0 when only aggregate performance against baselines is reported.
proposals.rationale: R22 compares vision encoders and feature levels, R36 systematically varies categorical and perceptual signals, and R60 compares objective-soup recipes.

proposals.name: Concrete reproducibility evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract provides usable, specific access to code, data, demos, or protocols supporting replication; score 0 when availability is merely promised conditionally, left vague, or uses a placeholder.
proposals.rationale: R03 gives a concrete source-code link and R31 provides code and demos, whereas R11 makes availability conditional and R53 gives only a placeholder.

proposals.name: Diagnostic benchmark validity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a benchmark is designed to separate meaningful capabilities, prevent leakage or redundancy, and produce interpretable failure analysis; score 0 when it is justified mainly by size or number of models.
proposals.rationale: R32 decomposes scientific-image understanding into compositional dimensions, while R51 filters uninformative and leaked samples; R15 mainly emphasizes benchmark scale and coverage.

proposals.name: Calibrated, limitation-aware claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states scope, failure modes, negative findings, or conditions under which claims hold; score 0 when broad superiority claims are presented without limitations or qualification.
proposals.rationale: R32 explicitly reports that all models struggle with complex prompts, and R47 reports that prior attacks fail at system level before identifying conditions that improve them.

proposals.name: Unifying abstraction across tasks
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a new abstraction explains and supports multiple previously separate settings with a common mechanism; score 0 when the method is a task-specific modification without transferable conceptual structure.
proposals.rationale: R04 unifies neural interactive-proof protocols, R52 frames diverse prediction tasks through a shared observer model, and R16 covers many penalty families in one optimization framework.

proposals.name: Constraints embedded in the objective
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when important real-world limitations such as sparse observations, weak feedback, or domain shift fundamentally shape the method and evaluation; score 0 when such constraints are mentioned only as motivation.
proposals.rationale: R07 incorporates planetary-navigation structure, R18 learns from preference feedback instead of scalar rewards, and R41 directly models cross-domain probability mismatch.

proposals.name: Justified simplicity with breadth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a compact design change has a clear rationale, is tested against strong baselines, and improves across several settings; score 0 when simplicity is asserted without explanation or broad evidence.
proposals.rationale: R28 uses a simple masking change with a concrete attention hypothesis, R42 builds MQL from three motivated ideas, and R49 achieves adaptive depth with minimal architectural changes.

proposals.name: Failure-to-mechanism fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposed mechanism directly targets a specifically diagnosed failure mode and the abstract explains why it should help; score 0 when the method is presented as a generic improvement without a problem-mechanism link.
proposals.rationale: The tight links between noise and inverse-Hessian estimation in R05 and distribution mismatch and latent regularization in R40 are substantive signals that generic scorecards may miss.

proposals.name: Reusable abstraction across task boundaries
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the paper identifies a shared principle that naturally spans substantially different tasks, datasets, or modalities and demonstrates that reuse; score 0 when the method remains task-specific despite broad wording.
proposals.rationale: R09 unifies seemingly unrelated prediction tasks through shared variable spaces, while R50 develops a general event-process kernel; both suggest conceptual breadth beyond checklist features.

proposals.name: Theory-to-experiment coupling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when theoretical analysis motivates concrete design choices and experiments directly test the predicted behavior; score 0 when theory and experiments are merely adjacent or the theory is decorative.
proposals.rationale: R05 connects inverse-Hessian approximation theory to noisy optimization experiments, and R43 connects residual-network stability theory to progressive training results.

proposals.name: Task or system boundary exposure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract reveals that the conventional task boundary hides an important failure and evaluates a formulation crossing that boundary; score 0 when it simply optimizes the established subtask.
proposals.rationale: R27 jointly localizes and repairs bugs instead of treating them sequentially, while R44 evaluates attacks at the closed-loop system level rather than only at a component.

proposals.name: Component-level causal attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract isolates individual components, comparisons, or design choices and shows which one causes which improvement; score 0 when a multi-component method is supported only by aggregate performance claims.
proposals.rationale: R01 separates uncertainty regularization from correlation labeling, and R20 compares shallow/deep and CLIP/DINO features before introducing feature merging; these expose causal structure more clearly than a single leaderboard result.

proposals.name: Evaluation validity for the stated capability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the evaluation directly measures the claimed capability, controls leakage or misleading metrics, and tests the relevant output distribution or context; score 0 when convenient benchmarks are only loosely related to the claim.
proposals.rationale: R37 removes uninformative and leaked samples, R38 replaces deterministic evaluation with distributional measurement, and R44 tests whether component-level attack effects actually produce system-level consequences.

proposals.name: Generalization under meaningful shift
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract demonstrates transfer to genuinely unseen domains, tasks, objects, distributions, or conditions and identifies what enables that transfer; score 0 when evidence is limited to related in-distribution test sets.
proposals.rationale: R09 transfers across disjoint input/output spaces, R17 handles novel concepts with few target images, and R41 targets newly encountered objects from sparse observations.

proposals.name: Matched resource-quality frontier
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when efficiency is quantified against a matched quality, compute, memory, data, or latency baseline and the trade-off is explicit; score 0 when efficiency is asserted vaguely or measured without a fair quality comparison.
proposals.rationale: R02 gives memory reductions at specified compute overhead, while R43 reports FLOP savings alongside downstream quality and R57 pairs millisecond latency with estimation accuracy.

proposals.name: Benchmark contribution completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a benchmark or dataset has a clearly motivated taxonomy, representative coverage, construction protocol, tasks, metrics, and baselines; score 0 when the contribution is mainly a name, size claim, or collection announcement.
proposals.rationale: R06 specifies an ability taxonomy, bilingual splits, and model analyses; R30 supplies a new dataset, multiple tasks, metrics, and public benchmarks; R37 explains curation and leakage filtering.

proposals.name: End-to-end operational realism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract evaluates under the constraints, feedback loops, interfaces, or consequences of the intended real-world use; score 0 when practical relevance is claimed but evidence comes only from isolated offline metrics.
proposals.rationale: R44 closes the loop through autonomous-driving behavior, and R57 reports real-time wearable inference across speeds and sensor placements; these contrast with application narratives such as R07 that provide less concrete operational evidence.

proposals.name: Boundary-condition honesty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states meaningful failure cases, limitations, or scope boundaries and calibrates its claims accordingly; score 0 when it uses sweeping superiority language without acknowledging where the method may fail.
proposals.rationale: R18 explicitly calls its rover results early training results, R25 reports that all evaluated models struggle with complex scientific prompts, and R31 shows that random search nearly matches the proposed search method.

proposals.name: Reproducibility substance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract provides concrete information about data, settings, tasks, metrics, comparisons, and artifacts sufficient to make replication plausible; score 0 when it offers only a generic promise that code or data will be released.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R06 rely heavily on future artifact-availability statements, whereas R30 and R52 provide unusually concrete dataset, task, modality, and benchmark descriptions; this separates substantive reproducibility evidence from an availability slogan.

proposals.name: Inspectability of the proposed mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method produces explicitly interpretable objects or programs whose meanings are defined and connected to the task, with an indicated way to inspect them; score 0 when interpretability is only an unsupported adjective.
proposals.rationale: R04 identifies partial attention with learnable basis functions, R10 produces executable programs for debugging, and R39 assigns specific meanings to network outputs and weights.

proposals.name: Principle extracted from comparisons
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when systematic comparisons yield a transferable scientific or algorithmic principle beyond the proposed model's score; score 0 when experiments only establish that one named method wins.
proposals.rationale: R20 extracts the surprising value of DINO and shallow features, R31 learns that random search is nearly competitive despite a complex evolutionary method, and R60 studies how distinct learning signals interact rather than merely ranking models.

proposals.name: Assumption-guarantee coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when assumptions are explicit, mildness is characterized, and the claimed guarantee precisely matches the problem and method; score 0 when formal guarantees are asserted without conditions or their relevance is unclear.
proposals.rationale: R19 states a smoothness condition for discrete robustness certification, R46 qualifies global convergence under mild conditions, and R55 ties its regret claim directly to preference-only feedback.
